questions.subject: English
questions.stem: Your school is holding an assembly to mark the anniversary of the day on which Nelson Mandela was sworn in as the first black President of South Africa. Write a speech of about 100 words for the Principal to deliver at that assembly, saying what the country gained by ending a system that separated people according to race.

markingPoints.description: Opens with a suitable greeting to the assembly and names the occasion.

Uses at least two concrete details of the day, such as the African National Congress winning 252 of the 400 seats, or dignitaries from more than 140 countries, or more than 100,000 people of all races celebrating in the streets.
Explains the change: a system that separated people according to race replaced by one that recognised the rights and freedoms of all peoples, regardless of the colour of their skin.
Ends with an appeal, such as Never, never again shall this beautiful land experience the oppression of one by another.
Uses a formal register, clear paragraphing and correct grammar and spelling.

answerScheme.modelAnswer:
Respected Principal, teachers and dear friends,
Today we gather to mark the anniversary of a day that changed a nation. On 10 May 1994 Nelson Mandela was sworn in as South Africa's first black President. His African National Congress had won 252 of the 400 seats in the first democratic elections, and dignitaries from more than 140 countries came to Pretoria. In the streets more than 100,000 people of all races sang and danced together. A system that separated people according to race was replaced by one that recognised the rights and freedoms of all peoples. Never, never again shall this beautiful land experience the oppression of one by another. Thank you.

questions.subject: English
questions.stem: Write a letter of about 100 words to the Principal of your school, dated 10 May, proposing one activity by which the school could mark the anniversary of the day the first black President of South Africa was sworn in, and giving your reasons.

markingPoints.description: Uses the right format: the date 10 May, a salutation to the Principal and a closing signature.
Proposes one clear activity for the assembly or the school ground.

Gives at least two reasons drawn from what that day achieved, such as the ending of a system that separated people according to race, the recognition of the rights and freedoms of all peoples, or people of all races celebrating together.
Keeps a polite, formal tone throughout and stays within about 100 words.
Uses correct grammar, spelling and punctuation, with no linking-word errors.

answerScheme.modelAnswer:
Dear Sir,
I am writing to suggest that our school mark the anniversary of 10 May, the day Nelson Mandela was sworn in as the first black President. I suggest that the whole school assemble in the ground at nine o'clock and that the first song be sung by all classes together. On that day a system that separated people according to race came to an end, and one that recognised the rights and freedoms of all peoples began instead. More than 100,000 people of all races then sang and danced together in the streets, so a joint assembly would show that idea in our own small way. I hope you will approve.
Yours obediently,
A Class 10 student

questions.subject: English
questions.stem: Write an article of about 100 words for your school magazine, with the heading Let Freedom Reign, on what the world gained on 10 May 1994.

markingPoints.description: Uses the article format: a suitable heading and a clear beginning, middle and end.
Mentions at least three facts of the day, such as 252 of the 400 seats won, dignitaries from more than 140 countries, and more than 100,000 people celebrating.
Explains that the new government recognised the rights and freedoms of all peoples, regardless of the colour of their skin.
Ends with a comment on why the day still matters to people today.
Keeps to about 100 words, in a clear style with correct grammar and spelling.

answerScheme.modelAnswer:
Let Freedom Reign
On 10 May 1994 a new nation began. In the first democratic elections in South Africa's history the African National Congress won 252 of the 400 seats. Dignitaries from more than 140 countries came to Pretoria for the inauguration, and more than 100,000 people of all races sang and danced with joy. A system which had separated people according to race was replaced by a government that recognised the rights and freedoms of all peoples, whatever the colour of their skin. Mandela had spent thirty years in prison for that change. The world gained proof that justice can win, and that is why this day still matters.

questions.stem: In about 120 words, and step by step, set out the pledge the writer makes to the Republic and its people, and the pledge he makes on behalf of all his people.

markingPoints.description: He pledged to obey and uphold the Constitution.

They pledged to liberate all their people from the continuing bondage of poverty.
And from deprivation, suffering, gender and other discrimination.
Never, never and never again shall the beautiful land experience the oppression of one by another.

answerScheme.modelAnswer: Step 1 - When it was his turn, he pledged to obey and uphold the Constitution of the new Republic. Step 4 - They pledged to liberate all their people from the continuing bondage of poverty. Step 5 - They pledged to free them also from deprivation, suffering, gender and other discrimination. Step 6 - They swore that never, never and never again should the beautiful land experience the oppression of one by another.

questions.subject: English
questions.stem: In about 120 words, and step by step, show how the writer's own experience in prison supports his claim that love, and not hate, is what people are born with.

markingPoints.description: No one is born hating another person because of the colour of his skin, or his background, or his religion.
People must learn to hate, and if they can learn to hate, they can be taught to love.
Love comes more naturally to the human heart than its opposite.
Even in the grimmest times in prison he saw a glimmer of humanity in one of the guards.
Perhaps just for a second, but it was enough to reassure him and keep him going.
Man's goodness is a flame that can be hidden but never extinguished.

answerScheme.modelAnswer: Step 1 - No one is born hating another person because of the colour of his skin, or his background, or his religion. Step 2 - People must learn to hate, and if they can learn to hate, they can be taught to love. Step 3 - Love comes more naturally to the human heart than its opposite. Step 4 - Even in the grimmest times in prison, when he and his comrades were pushed to their limits, he would see a glimmer of humanity in one of the guards. Step 5 - Perhaps just for a second, but it was enough to reassure him and keep him going. Step 6 - Man's goodness is a flame that can be hidden but never extinguished.

questions.subject: English
questions.stem: In about 120 words, and step by step, show why the writer found it almost impossible in South Africa to do his duty to his people and his duty to his family at the same time.

markingPoints.description: Every man has twin obligations: to his family, parents, wife and children, and to his people, community and country.
In a civil and humane society each man is able to fulfil both obligations according to his own inclinations and abilities.
But in a country like South Africa it was almost impossible for a man of his birth and colour to fulfil both.
A man of colour who attempted to live as a human being was punished and isolated.
A man who tried to fulfil his duty to his people was inevitably punished for it.
Each of the two obligations therefore brought punishment in that country.

answerScheme.modelAnswer: Step 1 - Every man has twin obligations: to his family, to his wife and children, and to his people, his community and his country. Step 2 - In a civil and humane society each man is able to fulfil both according to his own inclinations and abilities. Step 3 - But in South Africa it was almost impossible for a man of his birth and colour to fulfil both. Step 4 - A man of colour who attempted to live as a human being was punished and isolated. Step 5 - A man who tried to fulfil his duty to his people was inevitably punished for it. Step 6 - Each of the two obligations therefore brought punishment, so he could fulfil neither.
